#5565. MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?"

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

"Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

#5564. Opinion: If the AI bubble bursts, it could create a serious problem for health care

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Adler is chief scientific officer at the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine.

The Oct. 30 sell-off on Wall Street ignited doubts about whether the huge investment in artificial intelligence will earn the returns investors expect. Those concerns have persisted, with even Anthropic’s initial public offering on Nov. 19 failing to halt the broader tech sell-off.

If the AI bubble bursts (assuming it is a bubble) and takes some medical AI companies down with it, health care will face a serious problem. A health AI company’s market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things. If funding runs out because investors decide to walk away, hospitals could lose the chance to complete evaluations of potentially useful medical tools. Giving up on medical AI would be a financial decision — but it may look like a clinical one. The financial markets will decide which medical AI technologies survive before hospitals have had the opportunity to establish whether these technologies benefit patients.

If investment in medical AI technologies experiences a sharp fall, companies will lose funding, forcing them to reduce their activities or stop supporting their technologies completely. The impact of such an event could be felt across the entire health care system: Companies are developing AI tools ranging from interpreting scans to identifying patients at risk of developing medical complications due to treatments. Clearly, some of these tools will eventually prove useful in clinical settings, while others will not. The point is that neither an impressive AI tool nor a falling stock price tells us which AI tool deserves a place within the health care system.

To illustrate this point, let’s take cancer clinical trials as an example. In one study, researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Emory University examined electronic medical records using AI systems to identify patients who may meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in clinical trials. Determining eligibility involves a demanding manual screening process examining things like tumor characteristics, previous treatments, and lab results.

Interestingly, the findings revealed that using the AI system improved accuracy of assessing enrollment eligibility for the cancer clinical trials, but it didn’t reduce screening time significantly. It’s not clear whether such improvements would lead to an increase in patient enrollment. In another study, researchers in Australia from the Victorian Cancer Registry at Cancer Council Victoria and Monash Health utilized an AI system to analyze pathology reports with the goal of identifying patients eligible for enrollment in cancer clinical trials. The AI system was able to successfully identify more eligible patients when compared to standard screening procedures, but ultimately utilizing the AI system didn’t result in increased patient enrollment into the clinical trials. The study didn’t establish why, which brings to focus that screening improvements doesn’t necessarily lead to higher clinical trial participation.

Taken together, these two studies illustrate the potential utility of AI systems in health care. They also make clear that improvements are needed before such AI systems become an integral part of health care system.

Based on my experience in senior leadership in oncology drug development, I think that medical AI systems should be developed and evaluated based on the general framework that we currently apply in the research and development of new innovative cancer drugs. What I mean by that is when it comes to the AI systems promising early results are important, but it is critical not to celebrate a success too early. Ultimately the value of the AI system depends on whether it eventually benefits the patient. We need to determine whether using a particular medical AI leads to better clinical decisions, better patient identification, reduction of unnecessary work, or improved access to treatment.

If the AI bubble bursts, these success metrics could become more difficult to achieve. Companies developing medical AI systems may lose their funding, downsize, or even withdraw support for their products. Worst of all, they could close before hospitals have finished assessing their AI systems.

Clinicians could, of course, return to doing their work as they did before the introduction of the medical AI system. But that would mean the health care system loses the opportunity (and valuable data) to determine whether such medical AI tools could have offered meaningful improvements and patient impact.

The clear answer is not to try and save each struggling AI company, but to make sure that hospitals and health care system are able to complete their assessments of medical AI systems even if a given company reduces its services or even goes out of business.

Before adopting such medical AI systems, hospitals should establish clear success criteria and build systems in place to track, store, and ensure that the research data generated about the medical AI systems are available for independent evaluation even if the AI company supporting such a system no longer exists. Such plans would make sure that any financial difficulties that may affect a relevant AI company would not prevent the hospital or the health care system from determining whether a given medical AI system could benefit patients.

David Adler is chief scientific officer at the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine, with more than 15 years of experience in oncology research and drug development.

#5563. STAT+: Kymera Therapeutics reports mid-stage eczema trial success for would-be Dupixent rival

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

In a closely watched trial seen as one of this year’s most impactful immunology drug readouts, Kymera Therapeutics announced on Monday that its experimental therapy effectively and safely treated eczema patients’ itchy, inflamed skin.

In the Phase 2 trial, moderate-to-severe eczema patients randomly assigned to receive the biotech’s pill, KT-621, showed a statistically significant reduction in disease severity compared with those given a placebo. This was true across all three doses tested after 16 weeks of treatment, with a peak placebo-adjusted improvement of 45% among those given a moderate dose. Patients on this dose were also more likely to see an improvement of 75% or more in disease severity, with 62% of treated participants clearing that bar compared with 22% of the placebo group.

The BROADEN2 trial succeeded across all primary and secondary endpoints, including itch reduction and the fraction of patients who achieved clear or almost-clear skin. KT-621 was also generally safe and well tolerated. The only side effect that was more common among patients on the drug was conjunctivitis (i.e. pink eye), which appeared in 20%, 13%, and 11% of patients on a low, middle, and high dose, respectively. All of these cases were mild to moderate, and none caused participants to stop treatment.

#5562. Can ctDNA Help Guide Treatment Decisions in Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer?

— Experts discuss new ESMO findings and the limits of risk stratification

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest research presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this third of four episodes, they examine new findings about circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from KEYNOTE-B15, as well as its potential for predicting recurrence and the unanswered questions about using ctDNA to guide treatment decisions.

Click here to watch all episodes of this roundtable series.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: So let's talk a little bit about the next topic, which is ctDNA. And we saw ctDNA all over the place at ESMO this year, including in some high-profile presentations related to large randomized studies. So we're really starting to get, one, more data in the context of randomized studies, and two, we're beginning to see some data with different strategies for testing ctDNA after having had data really limited to what I'll call the standard Signatera assay for a while.

So let's talk about some of that data. So we saw data from KEYNOTE-B15, and remember KEYNOTE-B15 enrolled patients who were cisplatin-ineligible* with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, and patients were randomized to receive perioperative EV [enfortumab vedotin (Padcev)], pembro [pembrolizumab (Keytruda)], and cystectomy versus neoadjuvant gem-cis [gemcitabine and cisplatin] and cystectomy; ctDNA testing was done with the Signatera assay using the more standard approach in that study.And on the EV-pembro arm, there was an 82% rate of clearance of ctDNA from baseline to pre-cystectomy versus 66.7% with neoadjuvant gem-cis. [*Editor's note: KEYNOTE-B15 enrolled cisplatin-eligible patients.]

And presurgical ctDNA negativity did not absolutely predict a path CR [pathological complete response], but it was associated with a higher path CR rate and certainly was associated with more favorable event-free survival. We saw that in the post-cystectomy setting, the likelihood of having detectable ctDNA with modern treatment regimens and cystectomy was really pretty minuscule, in about the 5% range post-cystectomy. So Dr. Aggen, what do you make of that data and how do you use it in clinic?

Aggen: So I think it's exciting now that with a more sensitive whole-genome-based assay, 83% of patients pre-cystectomy are clearing their ctDNA. But the takeaway for me actually relates more to the other group that was positive pre-cystectomy. Even if they clear with surgery, that group is probably at a much higher risk of metastatic recurrence.

And so it does inform, for me, a patient with a positive ctDNA test before surgery is a patient who probably should be getting more adjuvant therapy. And so I think largely ctDNA in this setting is prognostic. We're trying to do the trials through Alliance to figure out if we can use that as a risk stratifier for those who have persistent positivity.

I think the other takeaway for me though, is that a negative test also doesn't mean that you're totally out of the woods. In the breakdown they showed by ctDNA status, the event-free survival at 2 years in the ctDNA-negative group was about 85 or 86%. So there's still a 15% chance that those patients recur.

So I think it's nice that we have this tool now for prognostication. I don't think it's quite there yet for how we risk stratify and it's not necessarily helping me to make a decision at this moment to deescalate therapy for patients.

Galsky: How about you, Dr. Berg? How do you use it? Is baseline ctDNA testing in muscle-invasive bladder cancer helpful? Does it help you decide who should get neoadjuvant treatment at all?

Berg: I do think so in the sense that when I think about ctDNA, and at least for perioperative therapy, you have your baseline, and then you have your post-treatment before surgery, and then you have your after treatment, and then you think about adjuvant treatment.

So a lot of the data, like Dr. Aggen was saying about being prognostic, is the patients that are just negative in the beginning at that first baseline test, they are doing very, very, very well. Going through the therapy, staying negative, having a good, probably, response, and then hopefully staying negative after that. Those patients we know we do well.

And I would emphasize, like Dr. Aggen was saying, if you're going into surgery still positive, that is something I think we can educate our patients really importantly about what that could mean, not to sway them away from potentially a curative surgery, but can have that discussion and then really follow it afterwards.

So I think it's really adding this extra layer for our conversations, probably can cause some anxiety and a lot more questions, but I think it's something that we are really building into our paradigm when we see our patients next to us and follow this real-time tracker with them. And it's exciting in a way, but also again, can make everyone feel very anxious. So I think when trials are coming in, we're going to really use that more.

And I know for your study, Dr. Galsky, how do we determine afterwards what we're doing with it? And do you need more if you're positive afterwards or can you go and have deescalate when you're negative? And what does that mean to be negative and stay negative, or positive to negative or negative to positive? It's a lot. It's a lot, but it's great to see all the data coming out and all the work being done in our large studies really adding that to the data. It really is, I think, so helpful for all of us because we all are using it so often in clinic.

Galsky: And we're just starting to scratch the surface regarding kinetics of change. So pre-cystectomy ctDNA detectability, like Dr. Aggen pointed out, it's probably not all created equally. And there are patients who are detectable prior to surgery who have a rising value. There are patients who are detectable prior to surgery having a declining value. And all of that probably matters somewhat, but we don't know how yet.

#5561. Industry Voices—The case for social prescribing in older adult care

Industry Voices—The case for social prescribing in older adult care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Loneliness and social isolation often show up in the exam room through an older patient’s high blood pressure, worsening depression or recent emergency department visit.

Lack of social connection is an increasingly common risk factor for both physical and mental health conditions that clinicians often recognize—but may not feel well-equipped to treat.

Approximately one in four older Americans is socially isolated, and more than four in 10 report feeling lonely. Both are associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality, including elevated risks of heart disease, stroke, cognitive decline and dementia. Social isolation is also associated with an additional $6.7 billion in Medicare spending, mainly from avoidable hospital and nursing home utilization.

As leaders of foundations committed to improving the health and well-being of older adults, we invest heavily in programs that foster social connection, especially for underserved populations. But to truly address this public health epidemic, healthcare providers must be part of the solution.

Clinicians can play an essential role in identifying lonely and isolated patients and referring them to resources that promote social engagement. Integrating social prescribing into clinical workflows presents challenges in the current U.S. payment system, but promising approaches are showing success and can be replicated.

Food as Medicine (FAM) programs have already expanded our understanding of what a prescription can encompass. While physicians regularly recommend that patients adopt a healthy diet, that advice is rarely heeded for both behavioral and socioeconomic reasons. What has made a difference is a clinician’s prescribing of free or affordable individualized interventions in partnership with community-based resources and with systemwide support.

Similarly, social prescribing is a structured, team-based intervention that involves assessing and addressing loneliness and social isolation as part of a patient’s care plan. Taking the patient’s individualized needs and circumstances into account, a referral is made to a community organization or program that fosters social connections. These activities can range from in-person group programs to virtual activities or telephone-based companionship for people with mobility or transportation barriers.

In the United Kingdom (U.K.), Canada and Australia, established social prescribing programs have been linked to reductions in emergency department visits, hospitalizations and healthcare spending.

Brief, validated assessment tools, such as the UCLA-3-Item Loneliness Scale and the condensed Berkman-Syme Social Network Index, can be incorporated into the routine patient health questionnaires to help identify those at risk. Hospitals have a new incentive to use these screens with the recently implemented Age-Friendly Hospital Measure from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which includes addressing social vulnerability as one of five required domains.

But what then? Identifying suitable programs, partnering with local organizations, and making those connections for patients is a job in itself, one that clinicians cannot reasonably be expected to add to their already full workload. And this is especially complicated in rural areas where both clinicians and programs are more likely to be limited.

In the U.K., they have designated “link workers” to fill this role. Here in the U.S., value-based care team practices, which are becoming more common, can support a similar position or share those responsibilities among team members. A Social Prescribing Learning Hub from Social Prescribing USA offers practical guidance for how providers can get started, including choosing community partners and models, measuring impact and navigating the insurance landscape.

The state of Connecticut has taken a different approach by building a social prescribing infrastructure in collaboration with SocialRx, a company that matches patients with appropriate programs, enabling healthcare providers to prescribe participation in arts and cultural activities that are free to state residents. Other states, including Georgia, Massachusetts and California, have developed similar social prescribing ecosystems.

Some insurers and care providers are creating their own social connection programs.  BCBS of Massachusetts has partnered with Elder Services of Worcester Area to reduce emergency department utilization among their Medicare Advantage members by providing Transition Coaches after hospitalizations or ED visits. The coaches screen patients for isolation and loneliness, connect them with social groups and companion visits, and help them use technology to stay connected with family, friends and healthcare providers.

Building a sustainable social prescribing infrastructure also requires government and philanthropic support for evidence-based programs that foster social connections in spaces where older adults commonly gather. One example is the American Library Association’s Aging Together initiative, supported by The John A. Hartford Foundation, which strengthens public library programs that reduce social isolation and promote older adults' health and well-being.

Other countries’ experience with social prescribing is building evidence of its effectiveness in improving social connectedness and health outcomes, as shown in a recently released evidence roundup from the Center for Health Care Strategies. However, more research is needed on how to implement effective social prescribing practices in the U.S. One such effort is a partnership between the Humana Foundation and the Aspen Institute to evaluate the prescribing, dosage and follow-up of relationship-building volunteer activities for diverse, underserved older adults who screen for loneliness or social isolation.

There is growing recognition of loneliness and social isolation as clinical risk factors impacting older adults’ health, independence and quality of life. Health professionals can play an essential role in identifying these risk factors and making social engagement a part of patients’ care plans. Support from health systems, philanthropy and the government is needed to staff and train teams, identify effective engagement strategies, build community partnerships, and establish pathways for referrals and follow-up. Working together, healthcare and community organizations can make social prescribing a practical component of age-friendly, whole-person care.

Tiffany Benjamin is CEO of the Humana Foundation. Rani E. Snyder is President of The John A. Hartford Foundation.

An experimental monoclonal antibody showed 70% to 90% protection against symptomatic Covid-19, Invivyd, a small biotech firm, said Monday.

The result, from a 2,359-volunteer clinical trial called DECLARATION, included three arms: a single 250-mg dose of the antibody, VYD2311; monthly doses of VYD2311; or a saline placebo. Results were released by press release. Invivyd said that it plans to file for accelerated approval for VYD2311 for preventing symptomatic Covid.During the pandemic, monoclonal antibodies were employed both as treatments and preventatives for Covid. The technology, however, fell into disuse as the market shrank and people gained protection against the infection. Still, Covid causes tens of thousands of deaths in the U.S., and Invivyd executives argued that there is a need for a monoclonal antibody. Moreover, they say, for some patients the monoclonal could be more effective than existing Covid vaccines. Covid vaccines reduced symptomatic infection by about 30%.

“Clinically, I really do believe that most Americans who are interested in using a pharmacological agent to protect themselves from Covid would probably move over to a monoclonal if given the option,” said Michael Mina, the former Harvard University infectious disease expert who is Invivyd’s chief medical officer. “And I think we’re going to aim to have volumes that can accommodate that over the coming couple of years.”

#5558. Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering new clues about how the heart changes over time.

In a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a new picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

"Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual."

Much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered important changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

"The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal said. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated."

Growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

Scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

The new analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as important centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

"To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal said. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging."

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts

Another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

Surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

"What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal said. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart."

The researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly important areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal said.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns

The study uncovered another important distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

In males, aging fibroblasts showed stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

However, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

Although the research does not yet identify a new treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

Rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

The experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

"Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta."

Together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

The research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

Materials provided by Jackson Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5556. Here's What I Learned After Administering Naloxone

— Comprehensive overdose education goes beyond just giving the drug

In my first year of college, I saw a man drifting out of consciousness at a city intersection. His breathing was slow, and his lips were blue. The New Haven winter nipped relentlessly at exposed skin, and part of me suspected hypothermia. But after a sternal rub failed to wake him, I administered the naloxone (Narcan) I had made a habit of carrying and used a CPR mask to deliver rescue breaths. Within minutes, he regained consciousness. As I reached for my phone to call a friend to bring water, the man said, "Please don't call the police. I'd love somebody to just sit with me."

Darman* was unhoused and an Afghanistan veteran living with post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). There are parts of his story that I may never fully grasp, even now as a medical student -- or even after a decade as a physician. What I did understand was the importance of having someone to lean on and seeing the full human beyond his emergency.

This year, my classmates in student government and I worked with faculty at Stanford University School of Medicine to make opioid overdose training a required part of the curriculum for every incoming class of medical and physician assistant students. Substance use curriculum in medical schools has historically focused on alcohol and tobacco, and a 2024 systematic review of 192 institutions found that only 9.4% had opioid use disorder training programs.

We also recruited an instructor with lived experience of substance use to lead the course. This is part of a larger point my peers and I hope to make: every medical trainee should graduate prepared to reverse an overdose and approach substance use without judgment.

The opioid epidemic was declared a public health emergency in October 2017, and has since claimed half a million American lives. Its earlier waves were driven by prescription opioids and then heroin; a third wave began around 2013, with substantial increases in deaths involving synthetic opioids, particularly illicitly manufactured fentanyl and its analogs. From 1999 through 2023, approximately 806,000 people died from opioid overdoses. Deaths have declined in recent years, with supply-side changes and community prevention efforts among likely contributors.

However, now is not the time to take our feet off the pedals. The opioid crisis is ongoing, and certain regions of the U.S. continue to be impacted disproportionately. Alongside upstream governmental policies and campaigns, medical schools therefore have a responsibility to continue the grassroots work of educating the next generation of clinicians. Institutions should work alongside students to integrate overdose-response training throughout the curriculum, ensuring that this education remains a sustained commitment rather than relying on individual student initiatives to carry it forward.

However, simply distributing harm reduction supplies, such as naloxone, is not enough. When the conversation stops at naloxone, we leave out education on what to do while the medication takes effect and how to care for the person when they regain consciousness. Comprehensive overdose education must address both. Opioids depress the central nervous system, slowing or stopping breathing and depriving vital organs of oxygen. Naloxone blocks opioids' effects at their receptors and can restore breathing within several minutes. In the meantime, responders need to know how to support breathing to help prevent brain injury.

At our training, students practiced on CPR manikins: opening the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin, creating a secure seal with a CPR mask to reduce mouth-to-mouth contact, performing breaths, and monitoring the chest. Current American Heart Association guidance recommends one rescue breath every 6 seconds for an adult who has a pulse but is not breathing normally; if a pulse cannot be confirmed, CPR is needed. Students should also learn to stay with the person until emergency help arrives. Naloxone can precipitate severe withdrawal, and the effects of some opioids such as fentanyl can outlive the medication, making additional doses necessary.

Following their training at Stanford Medicine, every student now receives a free naloxone kit and a CPR breathing mask. We also recently worked with a campus center to install a harm reduction dispenser at the medical school. Successfully responding to an overdose depends in part on having these supplies close and accessible.

As students, we become part of the community where we go to school. We drink coffee in its neighborhoods, walk its streets, shop in its stores, read on its park benches. For a few years, we make a life there. The people who share this community with us become our neighbors, including the ones whose lives rarely intersect with ours inside the university. Preparing to care for them is part of belonging to a place.

That night, I stayed with Darman in a park while he recovered before asking permission to bring him to Yale-New Haven Hospital. Medical training, I learned, does not make us immune to homelessness, addiction, illness, or loss. He and I, you and me, we are bound by humanity and separated by circumstance. Darman and I both liked hot coffee and video games. He was a father; I hoped to become one someday. We both tried to speak to our mothers as often as we could -- I over the phone, he in prayer.

Medical training will teach us to move quickly, to make decisions under pressure, to find the next thing that needs doing. I hope we also learn to recognize when someone needs us as a shoulder. Every medical school should prepare its students for that responsibility, and we can start by supporting one of America's most vulnerable populations: victims of the opioid epidemic.

Looking back on my 4 years at Yale, I think of that night with Darman as the first time I felt like a true New Havener. For a little while, in the winter cold, we had each other. Today, as a medical student 3,000 miles away in California, in a place I am still learning to call home, that moment reminds me time and again that it is love -- the action -- not necessarily love, the loud, or love, the promised, that makes this life worth living and trying for.

#5555. At first preventive services panel meeting in more than a year, votes are cast in private

By Amanda Erickson, Chelsea Cirruzzo, and O. Rose Broderick

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

Chelsea covers the Department of Health and Human Services with a particular focus on power and influence at the top. Confidential tips can be sent via Signal at chelseacirruzzo.42.

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

I’m taking a (very basic, 101) biochemistry course, and I spent much of the weekend trying to memorize the steps of glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. Metabolism is a beast, and I welcome your mnemonics!

In exchange, I offer a glimpse inside the two-day meeting of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which hasn’t met in more than a year. Members (many of them new and appointed by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) grappled with how to apply the Trump administration’s DEI rules to recommendations on cervical cancer screening and perinatal depression, among other things. Read on.

In its first meeting since March 2025, an influential panel of doctors that evaluates preventive medical care grappled with the ways Kennedy has upended science and medicine.

Last week, the 16-member panel voted on recommendations on screening for cervical cancer, perinatal depression, and unhealthy alcohol use by teens and adults. The recommendations have been awaiting completion for more than a year while Kennedy repeatedly canceled meetings and largely remade the panel’s membership.

The discussion was livestreamed to the public for the first time, though the votes were held in private. Throughout the session, longtime and new members debated a Trump administration policy requiring the removal of language on “diversity, equity, and inclusion,” after Roger Klein, director of the USPSTF’s parent organization, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, cut all sub-population data from recommendation language.

“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the topline may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” Alicia Fernandez, a member of the panel since 2025, said as members discussed cervical cancer screenings.

At another point, some members expressed concern about bias in the presentations from subject matter experts. Members also asked how they might accurately and transparently explain when and how artificial intelligence is used in their data and recommendations.

“Should our documentation say ‘supported by AI?’” new member Ronald Karlsberg asked. — Chelsea Cirruzzo

Over the last several months, the American Diabetes Association has been … a real mess. There have been recriminations, a raft of resignations, and a 1,221-member boycott. Who’s the loser in all this high drama?

Experts say the impact of the ADA’s crisis won’t be felt immediately. But a dysfunctional professional organization could stymie advances in diabetes care for years to come. That’s because the ADA plays a key role in setting guidelines and sharing research in journals and at wide-ranging meetings that attract thousands.

“All of this has coalesced to make everyone anxious, uncertain about the future of diabetes research,” one expert told STAT. “And the ADA should at this point be standing up and being something that we can all rally behind. Instead it is being fractured by its own actions.” Read more.

If you know the MAHA Institute, a think tank launched to support Kennedy’s agenda, it’s probably because of its roundtables.

Events, STAT’s Isa Cueto writes, are the organization’s “bread and butter.” They were also a money pit — one “Friends of MAHA” fundraiser cost $230,000 to put on and netted just $55,000 from three contributors.

That might help explain the group’s current financial troubles. As Isa reports, the Institute started 2025 with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, and ended the year with $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed last week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year. Read more, and also check out her companion piece on the MAHA PAC’s very odd spending habits.

When Eva Yi Xie moved to the U.S. from China in 2016, she spoke so little English she told her teachers she “probably won’t understand what you will talk about.”

But her biology teacher helped her bone up, giving her vocabulary lists and translated tests. By 2020, Xie was a Regeneron Science Talent Search finalist on her way to MIT. She has since become a rising star in science circles. As a graduate student at Princeton, Xie is combining neuroscience and AI to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions.

Xie was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last week while traveling home from a neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C. While her visa had expired, Xie’s lawyers said Xie has a pending asylum application and is in the U.S. legally.

The news has shaken academics across the country, who wonder if it’s safe for international scholars to travel to present their research. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people,” one said. “That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.” Read more.

Halfway through Friday’s meeting of the federal autism coordinating committee, where members discussed the most important scientific papers about autism in the last two years, Ginger Taylor was “very angry.”

“Committee members have been robbed of their statutory duties in having limitations on what can be submitted,” said Taylor, a parent of an autistic child and the former director of the Maine Coalition for Vaccine Choice. She wanted to add more than 200 articles from her personal archives that investigate whether vaccines can cause autism. (There’s no evidence they do.)

As they had during the previous meeting of the committee, which coordinates federal agency efforts to address autism and advises RFK Jr., Taylor and several other Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee members intermittently hijacked the gathering. They suggested the group, handpicked by RFK Jr., should include research on “immunological triggers” in its annual survey of important autism research.

If you want to read the more than 500 papers submitted by the public and committee members, you can find them here. Befitting the wide spectrum of autism, the papers diverge in topic and tone. The group will vote on which papers to include in coming weeks. These votes and the group’s strategic plan will act as guides for Congress as it allocates federal autism research funding. — O. Rose Broderick

A few years ago, Francesca E. Duncan received an unusual notice — one of her grant proposals to the NIH was being requested by a Chinese entity via the Freedom of Information Act. And by law, she had to share her scientific ideas.

Over the last decade, the NIH has received more than 13,300 requests for grant proposals, which “has significant negative ramifications on our society,” Duncan writes. “Scientific grants contain unpublished scientific data and sensitive intellectual property.” Read what happened next, and why Duncan believes we need more protections for unpublished scientific research.

#5554. How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout

How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Physician burnout may be falling nationally, but healthcare leaders are noting a potential new source of overwhelm: messaging overload.

And, it’s not affecting all providers equally.

Leaders at Ochsner Health, per the American Medical Association (AMA), found female physicians receive about 30% more staff messages and 30% more patient messages than their male counterparts through an analysis of electronic health record (EHR) data.

Though the direct causes are unknown, TigerConnect Chief Growth Officer Sheeza Hussain said general messaging overload is a “symptom of a coordination problem.”

“Healthcare slows down when people are waiting for information, decisions, consults, transfers, and discharges and all the handoffs in between,” Hussain said. “At TigerConnect, we focus on helping health systems remove those bottlenecks by connecting people, systems and workflows so communication moves care forward.”

Hussain continued, “When communication is orchestrated well, clinicians can focus on care, and patients can move through their care journey more smoothly and effectively.”

Hussain and Nikki Manuel, TigerConnect clinical solution design director, spoke with Fierce Healthcare about the factors driving this trend, impacts on patient experience and how health systems can mitigate it.

Editor’s note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

Fierce Healthcare: Why does message overload land unevenly in hospitals and health systems?

Nikki Manuel: Nurses are at the center of patient care and care coordination, so a significant share of the communication burden often falls on them. Think about a nurse trying to reach the right provider about a change in a patient’s condition. They may need to review the EHR, confirm who is on call, determine the preferred communication method and follow up if there is no response—all while managing other patients. The burden grows when communication crosses departments or shifts and ownership is unclear. The clinicians coordinating those handoffs can end up spending valuable time navigating the communication process instead of moving more quickly to the next step in care.

Sheeza Hussain: In my conversations with health system leaders, it comes back to fragmentation. Healthcare has never lacked technology, but more technology hasn’t created more connected care. Hospitals run single-purpose communication tools, fleets of devices, and disconnected biomedical equipment, putting out huge volumes of alerts and alarms. None of it coordinates, which puts clinicians in the role of middleware. It’s not a tool shortage. It’s a coordination problem.

FH: As this trend takes shape, who are the clinicians most affected by potential overload?

Hussain: Nurses, first. They’re asked to manually bridge disconnected systems and respond to alarms. Most alarms don’t need a response, but a nurse still has to hear every one to find out. Hospitalists and on-call physicians feel it too, especially when coverage isn’t clear. Clinicians should not be middleware.

FH: How, if at all, is messaging overload shaping up to be the next source of burnout for clinicians?

Manuel: I don’t think messaging itself is necessarily the next source of burnout. In many ways, messaging has made communication easier. As a bedside nurse, I remember relying on pagers and phone calls and having to stop what I was doing when a provider called back. Messaging gives clinicians more flexibility to communicate without constantly interrupting patient care.

The burden comes when we layer messaging onto communication processes that haven’t been standardized. Nurses are already surrounded by alerts, messages, and notifications coming from multiple systems, and they’re often the ones deciding what needs action, who needs to receive it, and what to do when there isn’t a response. That’s where the cognitive load starts to build.

Health systems should be looking at where communication can be standardized and where alerts, routing and escalation can be automated. Technology should support that process by identifying the appropriate person and helping get the right information to them without requiring a nurse to manually connect every step. Nurses shouldn’t have to serve as the middleware holding the communication process together.

Hussain: Because it adds to a load clinicians already carry. They’re surrounded by beeps, pings, messages and alerts, and most of it does not need action. The requirement to still read these messages and make that decision adds to cognitive overload and burnout.

It’s a thousand small interruptions compounded by the need to choose which tool to use to communicate. And the risk goes beyond burnout. When people tune out the noise, a real emergency can slip past. That’s a patient safety issue.

FH: Why do some organizations not have clear communication rules?

Manuel: Communication practices often evolve over time as organizations grow, add new technology and adapt workflows across different departments and care teams. That can naturally lead to different ways of communicating depending on the team, the workflow or even the situation. The important thing is establishing clear communication standards and governance around those practices.

Hussain: Many hospitals do not have clear communication rules because communication has evolved department by department and tool by tool, rather than as an enterprise-wide workflow strategy. Health systems have invested in a lot of technology, but more technology has not always translated into more coordinated care. The result is that a nurse, physician or operator may have to decide which system to use, who to contact, how urgent the issue is and what to do if there is no response. That is a lot of operational burden being pushed onto clinicians.

Clear communication rules are important, but they also have to be supported by technology that can operationalize those rules in real time.

FH: As messaging providers has become more commonplace at health systems, some have begun to charge for the service. How has that impacted overload, if at all?

Manuel: Research has shown that charging for certain patient messages can reduce message volume, but I don’t think we can assume that fewer messages automatically translates to less burden for clinicians.

We also have to consider the potential impact on patient access. We don’t want patients hesitating to reach out with questions or concerns because they’re unsure whether they’ll be charged. From a clinical perspective, the bigger question is whether we’re reducing the work associated with managing communication. If clinicians are still sorting through unnecessary messages, tracking down information or following up on requests that weren’t routed appropriately, we haven’t really addressed the underlying burden.

Charging may influence volume, but improving how communication is managed is what can make a meaningful difference.

FH: How does message overload ultimately affect patient experience and engagement?

Manuel: When we talk about message overload, I think the impact on patients is really about whether communication is helping care move forward or creating additional work and delays. When information is clear, actionable, and reaches the right person at the right time, clinicians can make decisions faster, reduce unnecessary delays, and keep care moving forward. When communication becomes fragmented or creates unnecessary noise, it can have the opposite effect.

Communication is also an important part of patient engagement. Patients want to understand what’s happening with their care, have their questions answered, and feel involved in decisions. When communication processes work well, clinicians have more time for those meaningful interactions and to apply their clinical judgment where it’s needed most. There’s also an element of confidence and trust. Patients may not see all of the communication happening behind the scenes, but they experience the result of it. When the care team is aligned, information is consistent, and next steps are clear, patients have greater confidence in their care and a better understanding of what to expect.

FH: How can leadership change communication without disrupting patient care?

Hussain: Leadership can start by treating communication as a patient-care-affecting workflow, not just a technology or etiquette opportunity. The goal is not to slow communication down or create more rules for clinicians to remember. The goal is to make communication more reliable so [that] the right information reaches the right person with the right level of urgency. That requires involving frontline clinicians, understanding where delays and interruptions are happening, and then standardizing the workflows that create the most friction. Done well, this should reduce disruption because clinicians are no longer forced to manually manage every handoff, escalation, or follow-up themselves.

FH: More broadly, what can hospitals and health systems do to mitigate this overload?

Hussain: Hospitals and health systems need to look at overload as a coordination problem. Clinicians are receiving messages, alerts, alarms and requests from many different systems, but those systems often are not working together. The first step is understanding where volume is coming from and which communications are truly actionable. From there, organizations can clarify escalation paths, reduce duplicative tools, and route communication based on role, schedule, urgency and context. Technology can help, but only if it is designed around the workflow.

FH: How could AI or other kinds of health tech provide relief for clinicians?

Hussain: AI and health tech can provide relief when they are built into real clinical workflows, not layered on top of them as another tool to manage. Clinicians do not need more alerts, inboxes or systems to check. They need technology that can reduce noise, understand urgency, identify the right person, and help activate the next step without forcing nurses, physicians or operators to manually coordinate it all.

This is where communication orchestration matters. The goal, and much of the work we focus on at TigerConnect, is to help health systems move from fragmented communication to smarter, role-based workflows that reach the right person at the right time. Used well, AI can help filter low-value communication, route information more precisely and automate routine coordination so clinicians can spend less time managing the work around care and more time with patients.

Good morning, Jason Mast here filling in from Pharmalot’s Midtown Bureau. Wishing you a happy Turkey week. I hope that it is joyful, or at least tolerable. In the meantime, the news marches on. …The FDA again rejected a hotly debated experimental Duchenne muscular dystrophy drug from Capricor Therapeutics, STAT tells us. The rejection letter came months after an advisory committee in which reviewers excoriated the company’s data, saying a Phase 3 trial had — contrary to Capricor’s claims — clearly failed. Some advocates and doctors pushed for the drug’s approval, noting it was for patients with a terminal disease and few other options.

Eli Lilly bought a U.K.-based Huntington’s disease startup for up to $725 million, Endpoints reports. The startup, called LoQus23 Therapeutics, is developing a pill aimed at an increasingly popular target in neurons called MSH3. LoQus23 planned to start a human trial in the coming months. This is Lilly’s 15th acquisition of the year, as its leaders look to pour obesity-drug riches into a new wave of powerful medicines.

Kymera said its closely watched Dupixent rival safely and effectively treated eczema in a Phase 2 study, STAT relays. The pill, called KT-621, targets an inflammatory protein called STAT6. It is among the first of a new kind of therapy called protein degraders that chemists and executives hope will let them target previously undruggable proteins. KT-621 has generated particular excitement among investors because of its potential to serve as an oral alternative to Dupixent, Sanofi and Regeneron’s mega-blockbuster immune drug.

#5552. Obscure CVD Billing Codes; Radiotracer Supply Recovers; Baby Heart Surgery Timing

— Recent developments of interest in cardiovascular medicine

Two highlights from a U.S. Government Accountability Office report of Medicare coverage for cardiovascular preventive services: Out-of-pocket costs can affect beneficiaries' use of specific services such as cardiac rehab, and many providers remain unaware of coverage for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk assessment and atherosclerotic CVD risk management.

The FDA alerted to a recall of certain vascular guidewires from Heraeus Medevio due to a potential issue with their hydrophilic coating. No related serious injuries or deaths have been reported to date.

Individuals with a genetic propensity towards high LDL cholesterol were at greater cardiovascular risk with more saturated fat intake in an observational analysis. (JACC: Advances)

In a cohort of adults with prehypertension, nearly half had masked hypertension, which was in turn linked to left ventricular hypertrophy. (JAMA Network Open)

Among low-risk individuals not on antihypertensive medication, elevated blood pressure was linked to a greater prevalence of silent atherosclerosis and more active atherosclerosis progression over 6 years. (European Journal of Preventive Cardiology)

Sotatercept (Winrevair), approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension, may work beyond pulmonary vascular unloading to exert direct myocardial protection in the right ventricle. (Circulation)

Researchers developed a cardiac electrical signal analysis model that may allow implantable cardioverter-defibrillators to anticipate a severe arrhythmia event months in advance. (Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology)

Following a shortage, Sun Radiopharma is back to producing the radiotracer Tc-99m pyrophosphate, according to an alert from the American Society of Nuclear Cardiology.

Maternal anemia and iron deficiency were associated with increased risk of acute heart failure during pregnancy and postpartum, an Indian case-control study found. (JAMA Cardiology)

It was feasible to implement pharmacogenomic testing prior to heart transplant so that patients get a list of actionable gene-drug interactions and dosage recommendations for tacrolimus, voriconazole, etc., a pilot study found. (Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation)

A meta-analysis indicated that after an embolic stroke of undetermined source, anticoagulation was no better for secondary prevention than aspirin, though people with left atrial enlargement leaned toward benefit in a subgroup analysis. (Lancet Neurology)

Habitual physical activity before and after stroke was associated with better mental health during recovery, a registry study showed. (Stroke)

The number of U.S. adult stroke survivors is expected to double to 20 million by the year 2050, the American Heart Association announced.

Body weight doesn't necessarily dictate optimal timing for most neonatal heart surgeries, registry data showed, the Norwood procedure and arterial switch operation being exceptions. (Annals of Thoracic Surgery)

#5551. Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."

Materials provided by Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
