#5549. Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'

Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medical associations and providers notched a legal victory over the federal government in a court ruling vacating federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

Those restrictions would have required recipients of Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care.

It was challenged by the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (HIVMA), the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in June (see that coverage below), who argued that the policy was contrary to Congress' intent when establishing the program under law in 1991, lacked sufficient explanation and discriminated against transgender people in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments.

The Nov. 19 decision from Judge William G. Young, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, prohibits the government from opposing its conditions in regard to all federal funding and permanently blocks any similar policies from being implemented by associational plaintifs' members, "which covers virtually every HIV care provider in the United States," said Lambda Legal, which acted as co-counsel for the plaintiffs.

"The ruling is a decisive and important victory for transgender people with HIV and protects the ability of physicians and other health care professionals to offer evidence-based care without political interference," Philip Bolduc, M.D., chair of HIVMA, said in a statement reacting to the decision.

Young's opinion and order opened with an acknowledgement that there are "sincere and deeply felt views" regarding transgender identity, and that the issue at question was of legal regulation rather than "the propriety of individual gender expression."

Still, the judge concluded his opinion by writing that the administration's conditions "are based in animus, loathing and discrimination. They do not stand for justice—in fact, they defy it. They are contrary to the laws of this nation and cannot continue to stand."

A group of medical associations and providers has filed a lawsuit challenging new federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

The new requirements, issued in a recent HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity, require recipients of the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care. The restrictions undermine the very intent of the program, the plaintiffs say, and violate anti-discrimination components of the Fifth Amendment.

“The Ryan White Program was created as a public health intervention to address the needs of low-income, vulnerable populations who otherwise would not have access to life-saving care,” Melanie Thompson, M.D., co-chair of a primary care guidance panel for the HIV Medicine Association, said in a press release. “It is crucial that Ryan White clinicians be allowed to continue to deliver the most scientifically appropriate treatments for all patients, including transgender individuals, without discrimination if we are to improve health outcomes for all and end the U.S. HIV epidemic."

The lawsuit alleges (PDF) that HHS and HRSA violated the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding their statutory authority and imposing restrictions that conflict with the Ryan White statute. The plaintiffs ask the court to block enforcement of the funding restrictions.

The case was filed by Lambda Legal and HSF Kramer on behalf of the American Academy of HIV Medicine, the HIV Medicine Association and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, plus two providers.

A preliminary hearing will likely be scheduled in a few weeks. Lambda Legal is “cautiously optimistic” about the future of the case, José Abrigo, senior attorney and HIV project director at Lambda Legal, told reporters on a webinar on Thursday afternoon. He called the administration’s actions “unlawful,” and said gender-affirming care in this context includes all types of care, including primary care and mental healthcare.

Specifically, the HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity reads: “Discretionary awards shall not be used to fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate … denial by the recipient of the sex binary in humans, or the belief that sex is a chosen or mutable characteristic.”

Some providers are already preemptively complying with the restrictions, Abrigo said, particularly in Tennessee and Kentucky. It is unclear how many other providers will also stop gender-affirming care. In certain cases, it’s up to individual states or departments of health to enforce the restrictions. It’s possible that medical records could be audited and reviewed for indications of pronouns, per Thompson. “It does matter what someone’s gender and pronouns are listed as,” Thompson said on the webinar, explaining that medical records are shared between providers and help ensure affirming care.

If a clinic is found to be non-compliant, the repercussions are steep, Thompson added. “The penalty for being found out is severe, and puts an entire program’s funding in jeopardy,” she said on the webinar.

Forty percent of American Academy of HIV Medicine members rely on Ryan White funding, of which 40% voluntarily report providing gender-affirming medical care. For low-income trans individuals with HIV, there aren’t many alternative options, per Abrigo. They may seek care through private insurance or potentially through Medicaid, but typically the population relies on Ryan White clinics for services.

Gender-affirming care restrictions under the Trump administration have been commonplace. Over 40 hospitals have reportedly stopped some gender-affirming care services for minors in response to pressure. Last week, the Cleveland Clinic promised the Department of Justice (DOJ) to commit $2 million to detransitioning services and a “decades-long” agreement not to perform gender-affirming care on minors. Delivering most of these services is currently illegal for minors under Ohio state law. Last month, DOJ struck a similar deal with Texas Children’s.

For months, experts have been sounding the alarm about the U.S. HIV response slipping into dangerous instability. In April, the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care (IAPAC) released a data brief finding that 61% of providers have reported at least one HIV service disruption and 68% have seen operational changes such as staffing reductions, service cutbacks and program closures. This was attributed to a combination of policy decisions, funding cuts and social determinants like loss of insurance coverage.

“It’s a catastrophe in the making," José M. Zúñiga, AIPAC's president and CEO, told reporters on the webinar. "It was already happening. This adds fuel."

#5548. New Option Approved for Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors

— Adding bezuclastinib to sunitinib improved median PFS by 7 months

The FDA approved the selective KIT inhibitor bezuclastinib (Ekitna), in combination with sunitinib (Sutent), for previously treated gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST).

The approval allows use of the combination in adults with advanced GIST previously treated with imatinib.

"With today's FDA approval of bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib, we have a new standard-of-care treatment following imatinib for patients with GIST," said Andrew Wagner, MD, PhD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, in an announcement from bezuclastinib-developer Cogent Biosciences. "This approval represents a major step forward for the GIST community and reflects the tireless progress made in improving the lives of people living with this disease."

Sara Rothschild, executive director of the GIST advocacy organization The Life Raft Group, called the approval "an incredibly meaningful milestone for the GIST community that has waited many years hoping, advocating, and helping advance the research for a new treatment option."

Principal support for the approval came from the randomized, international PEAK trial involving 413 patients with locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic GIST and disease progression after or intolerance to imatinib. Patients were randomized to sunitinib alone or in combination with bezuclastinib, and the primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) by independent review. Crossover to the combination was allowed after confirmed progression with single-agent sunitinib.

The primary analysis showed a median PFS of 16.5 months with the combination versus 9.2 months with sunitinib monotherapy. The difference translated into a 50% reduction in the PFS hazard (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.39-0.65, P<0.0001). Significantly more patients randomized to the combination achieved objective responses (46% vs 26%, P<0.0001). Overall survival data remained immature.

Adverse reactions to the combination occurring in ≥20% of patients consisted of diarrhea, increased liver enzymes, hypertension, dysgeusia, hair color changes, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, decreased appetite, stomatitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, rash, dyspepsia, and pyrexia. The most common (≥5%) grade 3/4 laboratory abnormalities were increased alanine aminotransferase and decreased leukocytes, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and hemoglobin.

The approval brings to six the number of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) for GIST. Imatinib remains the only TKI approved for first-line treatment. Sunitinib alone and the bezuclastinib-sunitinib combination are the only approved second-line therapies. Regorafenib (Stivarga) is approved for use in third line and ripretinib (Qinlock) for fourth line and beyond. Additionally, avapritinib (Ayvakit) has approval for unresectable/metastatic GIST harboring a PDGFRA exon 18 mutation.

Bezuclastinib also is being investigated as a potential treatment for systemic mastocytosis.

#5546. New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.

"This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," said Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being."

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD

Building on the initial findings, the research team plans to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a new way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need."

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable new tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

Other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

Materials provided by University of Texas at Austin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5545. STAT+: Medicare estimates $9.2 billion in savings from third round of negotiated drug prices

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

John Wilkerson, a Washington correspondent, is the author of D.C. Diagnosis, a twice-weekly newsletter about the politics and policy of health and medicine.

John writes about the politics of health care, and he is the author of the twice-weekly D.C. Diagnosis newsletter. You can reach John on Signal at John_Wilkerson.07.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect.

This is the third time the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices, which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years.

The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that established the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending.

#5544. Florida sues The Leapfrog Group for 'misrepresenting' its hospital safety grades to consumers

Florida sues The Leapfrog Group for 'misrepresenting' its hospital safety grades to consumers" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Florida’s attorney general has filed a lawsuit against hospital safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group alleging that it misled consumers about how it determines the grades assigned to hospitals, particularly those that declined to voluntarily submit data to the group.

The complaint, which was filed late last week and lists President and CEO Leah Binder alongside her organization, follows a similar suit brought by Tenet hospitals in the state that convinced a judge that nonparticipating hospitals were being “unfairly” penalized in Leapfrog’s methodology.

The group was ordered to withhold safety grades for those hospitals and in grade releases since has voluntarily chosen not to award ratings to hundreds of others that did not submit recent quality data to its surveys. Leapfrog appealed that decision in September, and has said it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

The Florida Office of Attorney General James Uthmeier’s lawsuit cites that case. It argues that Leapfrog’s poor scores for “at least seven Florida hospitals” misled patients, and outlined specific cases in which patients had declined care over the perceived poor performances of those hospitals.

“The Leapfrog Group told Florida patients its hospital grades were peer-reviewed and backed by experts. That was a lie,” Uthmeier said in a Friday release announcing the litigation. “When hospitals declined to fill out its survey, Leapfrog handed them the worst scores in the country without a shred of data, and patients refused surgery because of it. Leapfrog and its CEO should expect to be held accountable.”

The office requested that the court permanently bar Leapfrog from “misrepresenting to Florida consumers … the data, sources, methods or expert approvals underlying any hospital grade or score they publish,” or from representing the scores as peer reviewed. It also seeks to limit Leapfrog’s solicitation of charitable contributions, make corrective disclosures, and pay out other relief to providers, patients or other affected individuals and groups.

Leapfrog, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said the office’s case “poses the specter of outright government censorship,” and was “piggybacking” on the Tenet hospitals’ case “with old allegations Leapfrog strongly refuted.”

“Leapfrog looks forward to answering in court and defending our First Amendment rights and most importantly, patient safety,” the group’s statement reads. “Too many patients are harmed or killed by medical errors and infections in hospitals, and Leapfrog will always stand up for their lives as we have for 26 years.”

The methodology change at the heart of the cases came ahead of Leapfrog’s fall 2024 safety grade publication. It more heavily weighed “imputed” scores for four of Leapfrog’s 32 safety measures that were assigned when recent safety data for the two preceding years were unavailable. The Tenet hospitals, in their case, highlighted internal communications and other testimony that questioned the validity of the changes. Both lawsuits suggest the changes were made to maximize hospital participation in Leapfrog’s survey, which would bring downstream increases to revenues it collects from allowing hospitals to advertise their grades.

Uthmeier’s office has also filed a friend of the court brief to the appellate court now considering Leapfrog’s appeal, where it similarly argues that Leapfrog’s conduct is a violation of Florida’s consumer protection laws and not protected by the First Amendment.

The new complaint comes the same week as Leapfrog’s latest hospital safety grade release, which, similar to the spring release, withheld grades for 447 hospitals.

#5543. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5542. AI Helped Hospital Lower Readmissions, Deaths After Discharge

— EMR-based tool alerted clinicians to highest-risk patients in need of closer follow-up

Artificial intelligence (AI) helped one Texas hospital lower readmissions and post-discharge deaths, without adding any new staff, according to a case study presented at the HLTH conference in Las Vegas.

Using predictive AI to focus follow-up visits on its Medicare surgical patients at highest risk, Houston Methodist Hospital's 30-day post-discharge mortality fell about 35%, and readmissions fell about 18%, Brenda Campbell, MS, BSN, the hospital's senior innovation consultant, said at the conference.

Observed-to-expected (O/E) ratios -- which compare patients' results with those of Medicare patients matched for baseline risk -- fell from 0.48 in 2021-2022 to 0.31 in 2025-Q1 2026 (a partial period) for post-discharge deaths. Meanwhile, the O/E ratio for readmissions fell from 1.17 to 0.96 over the same period. A falling O/E ratio means the hospital moved faster than the benchmark, she reported.

Clinician follow-up visits within 14 days rose from 54.6% to 62.2% in the highest mortality-risk group and from 55.8% to 64.5% in the highest readmission-risk group during that time. Crucially, the hospital said this was accomplished without adding staff.

"We've done this without any additional resources," Campbell said. "Resources are tight. ... You have to really risk-stratify to get the right patients to the resources that you have."

The effort began in 2021, when Houston Methodist Hospital asked why its cardiovascular service line ranked well for inpatient mortality but poorly after discharge. The hospital brought in the Health Data Analytics Institute (HDAI), which had trained predictive AI on the entire Medicare data set, including 150 million Medicare lives.

HDAI found the cardiovascular service line ranked 7th for in-hospital mortality but 43rd for 30-day post-discharge mortality among more than 100 academic medical centers. About 70% of the 30-day post-discharge deaths occurred in the highest-risk quintile of patients.

"You can't manage what you don't know," Campbell said.

The hospital created a risk stratification plan, with predictions embedded into the electronic medical record. It asked clinicians to prioritize follow-up within 2 weeks for the highest-risk patients.

"Your limited team can't see everybody. ... So let's get to the people who are most likely to readmit," Carola Endicott, EdM, vice president of customer engagement at HDAI, said at the conference.

Timely follow-up can be life-saving, Endicott said in an interview after the session. A patient might be experiencing shortness of breath they don't feel is urgent enough to call about, she said. They may have forgotten to pick up a potentially crucial prescription medication, and need a friendly reminder. Or perhaps there was a surgical complication that wasn't caught.

John Brownstein, PhD, senior vice president and chief innovation officer at Boston Children's Hospital, who was not involved in the initiative, called it a "really concrete application of AI to predict high-risk groups that are worthy of intervention in a way that reduces the risk of readmission and mortality."

"AI can level the playing field," Brownstein told MedPage Today. "Well-funded health systems can hire staff to compensate for some of these challenges, but in a world where you are understaffed, AI can help reach those goals."

By working with clinicians to prioritize efforts, Houston Methodist Hospital's readmission ranking among 114 academic medical centers, among all medical and surgical Medicare fee-for-service patients, rose from 59th in 2022 to 7th in 2024, based on actual-to-expected rates, Campbell reported.

Mortality and readmission post-discharge is a major metric that hospitals track, said Brownstein. "It's a big cost to health systems and it is a big impact for patients. That's why so many health systems have invested in this space."

For Brownstein, this case study shows that implementing AI solutions doesn't have to be overcomplicated. "We want the right tool for the right problem. We over-index on these high-token use cases for generative AI. In this case, this use case is straightforward, and really high-value."

"We think it's the small things really that can have the biggest impact," Campbell said. She would like to see the follow-up rate climb further. "We're not where we want to be, but we know we're on the right trajectory to get there."

#5541. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

#5540. Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes

Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Late last week, the Trump administration released a proposed rule that includes a slew of technical changes in Medicare Advantage for 2028, citing enhanced competition as a key goal.

Analysts dove into the beefy regulation and projected that changes to MA's star ratings program would likely cull more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

Per a note from Leerink Partners, estimates from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services suggest that the changes would cut federal spending by $11.5 billion in 2031 and $107 billion through 2037.

The Leerink analysts estimate that about 58% of Medicare Advantage contracts would see lower scores using the newly proposed methodology, with about 20% of contracts losing quality bonus payments, which are tied to star ratings performance.

In the rule, CMS proposed moving to a set of 15 measures to determine the star ratings scores, which are focused on member experience and outcomes. The proposed rule would also eliminate the Reward Factor, and in tandem, these changes "would remove a cushion for contracts sitting at the critical QBP threshold, while concentrating performance across fewer measures," according to the Leerink report.

The analysts said that the potential impact of these proposals "reminds us just how many plans have been living at 4 stars for years with the hugely important Reward Factor."

The report estimates that the changes to the star ratings, if finalized, would have an uneven impact on insurers. For example, Humana would see the number of contracts earning four or more stars decline from 95% to 82.9%. Clover Health, meanwhile, would likely maintain 100% of its contracts, earning at least four stars.

UnitedHealthcare, by comparison, could see a drop from having 67.9% of its contracts in plans with at least four stars in 2027 to just 8.8% under the new methodology. For Aetna, the Leerink analysts project a decrease from 70% to 0%.

Given the scale of the changes, the Leerink analysts write that the rule sets the stage for a significant overhaul of the policies and rules that govern Medicare Advantage. The proposal is "almost overwhelming in size, scope and the impact on the industry."

Molly Turco, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in a note Monday that the proposed rule "is more significant than expected, in both revenue impact and scope and touches most core aspects of MA."

"It appears CMS aimed to reform long-standing concerns, especially Stars, in a way that takes money out of the program, while also loosening regulation on things like agents/brokers, seamless enrollment, network adequacy, etc. to help the program grow," Turco wrote. "However, we think these growth/deregulation policies are unlikely to offset the headwinds for MA."

She noted that while most of the most painful changes wouldn't impact plans until 2031 at the earliest; the delay does suggest CMS may be comfortable including more significant short-term changes to risk adjustment in the forthcoming 2028 Advance Notice, which is expected in January.

Ryan Langston, an equity research analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in the note that the proposed rule would likely be net negative for insurers with large, multi-state contracts and more people enrolled with plans earning at least four stars.

The delayed timeline of at least four years does grant plans time to adapt, Langston wrote, but the financial impacts would likely force benefit changes. The proposed rule could also spook investors concerned about what's included in the 2028 rate notice, he said.

"The combination of a smaller measure set, elimination of reward factors and reduced improvement measure protection likely lower Star ratings across the industry and force plans to mitigate lost revenue via benefit revisions," Langston wrote.

The Leerink analysts wrote that health plans are almost certain to fight the regulation. Lawsuits have become commonplace in the stars space, with multiple payers suing the feds over the most recent round of scores.

"We believe a lot of what has been proposed will change and/or not be implemented at all," they wrote. "Expect industry litigation."

#5537. HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth

HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Rural hospitals claim a relatively small portion of the state-directed payments being squeezed in coming years by 2025’s H.R. 1, with much of the legislation’s projected spending reductions the result of holding funds for those hospitals from growing beyond fiscal year 2025 levels, Department of Health and Human Services policy heads wrote in a new report.

The analysis, released Monday, paints a softer picture of the rate limits Republicans imposed on a supplemental Medicaid payment stream in last year’s broad budget reconciliation law, also referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or the Working Families Tax Cut Legislation.

Hospitals and other healthcare industry groups, as well as advocates and Democrats, have said the law’s billions in projected savings—from state-directed payment changes as well as other policy areas like Medicaid work requirements—are likely to devastate providers already operating at thin or negative margins.

Specifically, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)’s analysis showed that an estimated 7.8% of Medicaid state-directed payments reached rural hospitals in FY2025, or $11.5 billion out of $148.3 billion. That rate is slightly above rural hospitals’ 7% share of total Medicaid hospital spending for that same fiscal year, as estimated by the CMS Office of the Actuary.

Scaling from that baseline in line with H.R. 1’s multi-year payment rate phasedown, with some cumulative adjustments, showed that total nominal cumulative spending on rural state-directed payments would decline by 42.9%, or $81.6 billion, from 2026 through 2035 under the bill. This rate is again slightly higher than the CMS Office of the Actuary’s 40.8% estimate for all affected hospitals, which ASPE said is the result of the higher average dollar weighted payment rates rural hospitals currently receive, “which means that rural providers have more room to reduce rates to meet the new limits of 100% to 110% of Medicare.”

The ASPE report’s bottom line, however, is that $75.2 billion of the $81.6 billion reduction rural hospitals face, or 92.1%, reflects projected increases over the FY2025 baseline of $11.5 billion. The remainder, about 7.9% of the projected change, is a reduction below FY2025’s estimated state-directed payments to rural hospitals.

HHS, in a release highlighting the report’s findings, said that the language used in government reports describing the full $81.6 billion 10-year spending reduction as “savings” misses the government’s primary goal of capping future growth.

“Counting every dollar of projected savings as a cut below existing funding gives the public the wrong picture. Most of these savings are not reductions below what the program spent in 2025,” HHS Chief Economist and Chief Regulatory Officer Casey Mulligan, who was one of the report’s coauthors, said in the release. “They reflect future spending increases that will no longer occur. Our analysis makes that distinction clear.”

H.R. 1’s multi-year scale down in state-directed payment rates is set to begin in 2028, and are expected to slash some hard-hit states’ Medicaid spending by up to a quarter of their total annual Medicaid spending, per one analysis. Hospitals have broadly criticized the policy changes while spending much of this year adjusting their operations to contend with the future limits supplemental revenue, expectations of increased uncompensated care costs and year-to-year expense pressures like wage and supply inflation.

Additionally, CMS earlier this year proposed state directed payment caps substantially more extensive than what was outlined in H.R. 1 and used as the basis for Monday’s ASPE report. That proposal would extend rate limits beyond the bill’s four outlined service areas (inpatient hospital services, outpatient hospital services, nursing facility services and qualified practitioner services at an academic medical center) to “all [state-directed payments]s for all services in all states.” Hospital groups have flatly opposed the proposal, which more than triples the 10-year estimated savings.

Lawmakers last year, when seeking votes, blunted H.R. 1's funding reductions for rural hospitals by inserting a five-year, $50 billion rural health fund into the legislation. Those funds have come with usage restrictions for states and providers, with critics also noting transparency concerns and the fund's relatively small scale compared to the bill's total projected impact on hospitals.

It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime. On this summer Wednesday, a neurointerventionalist in Anchorage got the alert: Three hundred miles away, at a hospital deep in Alaska’s interior, a clot in a major artery was blocking the flow of blood to a patient’s brain. He needed it out — and he’d have to come to the state’s biggest city to get it done.

Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots.

In his mid-60s, the patient on the doctor’s phone had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. Like most patients with stroke symptoms, he got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke, whether it’s caused by a clot or a brain bleed, and determine whether that clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally, once the scan is complete, it could take 45 precious minutes just to send those thousands of two-dimensional brain snapshots to Anchorage for review — 90 million brain cells before a doctor could accept his transfer.

But this summer day, the patient had a new type of technology on his team. Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the United States, the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain, and survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients. In recent years, states have built up stroke networks, including telestroke care and automated artificial intelligence analysis, to try to improve transfer times for patients without access to specialist neurological care. One of the latest additions was in Alaska — where, starting in 2023, a small network of hospitals had agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care, faster.

Nearly instantly, the tool, from RapidAI, analyzed his CT scan for signs of a large vessel occlusion, or LVO, a type of blockage that often needs to be mechanically sucked out or retrieved with a stent. Through an app used by other hospitals with the technology, the results went out to his local team of doctors and the faraway network of neurointerventionalists — one of whom was on call at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.

The app alerted the doctor with the results just seconds after the scan was complete: suspected LVO. Less than a half hour after the patient arrived at his local ER, the team had called Providence for a transfer — two minutes before their on-call radiologist even delivered their official CT report.

Four hours and 23 minutes later, the clot was out. Without the AI assist, it would have taken at least an extra hour.

In 2026, it’s not rare for a hospital to use AI to triage stroke patients. Eight years ago, clinical trials showed that automated image analysis could extend the clot removal window for stroke patients as late as 24 hours after they were last well — before this, the window was just six hours. At the same time, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first AI to detect large vessel occlusions.

Those “were the wonder years,” said Stanford neurologist Greg Albers, co-founder of RapidAI. “Stroke centers scrambled to access the software.” Developers started to bundle different stroke algorithms in one package, driven by vendors like Viz.ai, Aidoc, and Brainomix, along with RapidAI.

As with most new medical technology, though, that adoption has been uneven. At the forefront of the deployment were large metropolitan hospitals, including those categorized as comprehensive stroke centers.

“Maybe it’s because they had more advanced workflows in place. Maybe it’s because they had the funding to acquire this AI software,” said Casey Pelzl, a researcher at the Harvey L. Neiman Health Policy Institution who studied some of the technology’s early adoption. “But what we know about stroke is that a lot of patients seek initial treatment at noncomprehensive stroke care centers, and these are the places that could potentially benefit from it the most.”

That’s the promise that a small group of stroke coordinators and neurointerventionalists in Alaska saw in 2023, when they established a volunteer nonprofit called the Alaska Stroke Coalition in a bid to improve stroke outcomes in a state that throws up obstacles at every turn.

“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, Providence’s stroke program manager. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. The state doesn’t have consistent reporting of stroke outcomes. And in the summer months, when cruise ships wind up the coast, a seaside hub’s population can swell nearly tenfold, often enriched with older passengers. Jaded hospital workers sometimes call them the “stroke boats.”

Against those unfavorable odds, one thing that could improve patients’ chances of survival after a stroke is getting them to the right care as fast as possible. “‘Time is brain’ is still very much the case, and the more quickly you can start a treatment — whether it’s the drug to break up the clot or if it’s a big clot, to transport them where they can get the clot taken out — that’s going to make a big difference for people,” said UC Health neurologist and stroke researcher Joseph Broderick.

By 2023, a few hospitals in the state, mostly in Anchorage, had started using RapidAI’s software, but barely any regional hospitals in the state’s interior and on its far-flung coasts did. Even for those hospitals that had the tech, “the challenge was we existed in all these different systems, but we weren’t coordinated,” said David Stoffel, RapidAI’s chief business officer. Each hospital had its own software license and didn’t share information within the app, making it difficult to coordinate decision-making for patients who might have needed a transfer.

So the newly formed Alaska Stroke Coalition, whose founders included Isaacs, tried to build a solution. Lucy He, a neurointerventionalist in Alaska, found funding from a family foundation to buy RapidAI for six additional hospitals spread across the state, at a cost of about $450,000. The resulting network spread from Alaska’s very northernmost tip in Utqiagvik, all the way south to the state’s capital of Juneau, which can only be accessed by air or water. When the tech threw up an alert about possible LVO in a patient, the message wouldn’t just circulate within that hospital team — it would go out wide, to the neurointerventionalists in Anchorage who might be able to help.

In return for the coalition paying for the AI tool, the health systems agreed to report their performance over the next three years, to see if the technology could really make a difference.

Day to day, the stroke coordinators and doctors accepting patients from across the state saw the technology changing their decision-making. It wasn’t always about quickly transferring patients for treatment — sometimes it was about making the hard calls to stay put.

Kevin Myrick, one of the coalition’s founders and Providence’s stroke program coordinator, pointed to a patient transferred to Providence this summer: a man in his 80s with a large vessel occlusion and severe symptoms. Patients like him are usually paralyzed on one side and lose speech. When strokes are this bad, it is far from given that a patient will regain function after treatment: Dead brain tissue is dead, forever. And restoring blood flow to dead tissue can do more harm than good, reintroducing toxic metabolic byproducts into circulation and causing swelling and bleeding.

“We did not put this [technology] in to transfer every patient to Anchorage,” said Myrick. If a patient doesn’t have enough chance for recovery, it can be preferable to keep them closer to home — to save them expense, keep them near their support network, and avoid using limited EMS staff time and planes.

In these cases, it’s a head CT with a contrast agent showing detailed blood flow in the brain that can help doctors tell what intervention is worthwhile. In the Rapid app, that image looks like a series of brain slices colored in neon-bright, Lisa Frank shades of green and pink. Pink tissue is gone. Green is brain that has the potential to be salvaged if blood flow is restored in time. “In Alaska, where you’ve got those big distances, having that imaging is going to be really important about deciding who to send and why to send,” said Broderick, of UC Health.

For the patient in his 80s, the CT perfusion images that came through the app showed far more green tissue than pink, their volumes neatly tabulated in milliliters by the software. “This patient was definitely a go,” said Myrick. He traveled 750 miles — about the distance from New York City to Chicago — and within a few minutes of arrival was shuttled into Providence’s catheterization lab, its team ready and waiting.

A CT scan after the clot removal shows his brain in profile. Blood fills the main arteries and tangled branches that supply oxygen throughout the entire brain; in his first CT, nearly half of that field was blank, its roadways cut off by the clot. Still weak and with impaired speech after the mechanical thrombectomy, he has a long way to go, said Isaacs. But “when he got sent home, he’s got a much better chance of recovery than he would have otherwise.”

The technology isn’t perfect. Like most radiology algorithms, there are false positives — scans that the app will say show a large vessel occlusion that actually don’t. It takes a good image to work well, said Broderick: “Sometimes, when you look at the pictures, if the person moves or the study wasn’t done right, the data is not good.” That means a doctor still reviews every output, and that official read is what drives the call to transfer or not. And for the biggest returns, it requires a hospital to actually perform CT perfusion imaging, which hasn’t been uniformly adopted in hospitals that don’t remove clots themselves.

But despite the limitations, the hospitals that have received the technology through the coalition’s grant are enthusiastic about connecting more of Alaska with the same alert system. “In rural Alaska, at all these tribal health organization hospitals, I think that that really can change the narrative here,” said Dylan Latif, stroke coordinator at Alaska Native Medical Center, one of the program’s grantees, at a meeting of the coalition in early October.

“If we do this with a bunch of different hospitals, then we create, you know, the Skynet of stroke in Alaska,” said He, the neurointerventionalist, at the same meeting.

The stroke coalition hasn’t yet published research about how the technology has impacted stroke care for Alaskans. But early data point to a recent increase in the number of thrombectomies delivered in Alaska, which could be driven in part by the program. And once patients arrived in Anchorage, hospitals with cath labs saw about a 30% improvement in the time it takes to start threading a device in to retrieve a clot.

“Logistically, every cath lab in America during normal business hours is booked 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. all day, every day,” Isaacs explained. With coordinated alerts from referring hospitals, it can be easier to prepare for stroke patients’ arrival. “We’ve got our little flight tracker up, and we’re like, OK, they’re 30 minutes out,” she said.

As is so often the case with AI deployed in health care, it will be longer before Alaska can show whether the new technology is changing the outcomes that matter the most: rates of long-term disability and death from strokes. It’s especially challenging in Alaska, where detailed data has been scarce; more complete stroke intervention and outcome recording began at the same time the coalition expanded the use of AI.

“Can I give you statistically significant information that RapidAI has made a big difference in the state of Alaska?” said Isaacs. “I can’t, really.”

For now, some doctors who care for stroke patients in Alaska are optimistic. “Being able to take these people who are from way the heck out of the middle of nowhere, they got 45 minutes to the local scanner, and now they are deemed eligible for an intervention — it has saved countless numbers of patients,” said Ryan Wilson, a neurologist at Alaska Native Medical Center, to his colleagues during the October meeting. “They’re gaining their brain back.”

As the members of the Alaska Stroke Coalition face down the end of their three-year grant period, that enthusiasm is translating into action: Each one of the six hospitals that got free access to RapidAI has said it wants to keep and pay for it. And there’s hope for even more significant changes to the landscape of stroke care in the state.

“Coincidentally, three things happened that help us further that mission,” said Isaacs.

The first happened this February, when the American Heart Association and the American Stroke Association released new stroke guidelines. The previous guidelines suggested narrow windows in which a patient could be treated with clot-busting drugs: They had 4 1/2 hours to get the medication. But in the updated guidelines, depending on how much salvageable tissue a patient appears to have in one of those pink-and-green CT perfusion images, they can still receive the drugs nine, even 24 hours after symptoms started.

That could dramatically increase the number of treatable stroke patients in Alaska — especially those who can be treated in place by clot-busting drugs. With RapidAI in more hospitals, Isaacs hopes that perfusion imaging will become more common, helping to make those calls about whether a patient falls in those extended windows. “Stroke used to be way more depressing to take care of, because our treatment options were very limited,” she said. “The windows were very short, and now with increased technology and increased time in our guidelines, it’s not quite as sad as it used to be, honestly.”

The second boost came in June, when Alaska enacted a law that will help establish statewide standards for strokes and heart attacks, like it already had in place for trauma. “We always sort of looked over at what trauma had, and we were like, ‘Isn’t that great? They’ve got designations, they get site visits, they’ve got data collection. We need these things,’” said Isaacs, who, along with several other coalition members, voiced support for the bill.

And in October, the final piece of the puzzle fell into place: The coalition got word that the work it’s been doing is primed to expand. “They got proof of concept that they can achieve this equity of care in Alaska for stroke,” said RapidAI’s Stoffel, and leveraged it in an application to the five-year, $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program.

In the first year of funding, the Alaska Stroke Coalition received $3.2 million of the state’s funding to start building a statewide AI imaging network.

With grant-funded hospitals and independent purchases combined, Alaska will soon have 21 acute care hospitals and two CT scan-enabled clinics with RapidAI’s stroke system in place. “This is phenomenal for Alaska,” said RapidAI’s Albers. “There are financial issues for some of these smaller hospitals, and I think they’re even more significant in Alaska than elsewhere.”

The group hopes to receive funding for at least two more years — first, to build support infrastructure that allows for rapid decisions to transfer or keep patients, and then track the financial impact of the technology on hospitals.

“As a girl who was born and raised in Alaska, this is the most Alaskan story that you can get,” Isaacs said to the room of her colleagues in the coalition’s October meeting. Earlier that day, she had gotten the email confirming the grant funding. “It’s like, ‘Oh, you don’t want to do it? Fine, we’ll go do it ourselves.’ And here we are.”

#5535. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Original written by W.B. Kagan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5534. Less Intensive Follow-Up of Lung Nodules May Result in Larger Cancers

— Study suggests a return to more intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules

A less intensive approach to monitoring newly detected small lung nodules failed to meet noninferiority criteria compared with a more intensive strategy, and may result in larger cancers at diagnosis, a cluster randomized pragmatic trial showed.

Among the patients with lung cancer, 36.3% of those in the less intensive group had cancers larger than 20 mm at diagnosis compared with 27.7% in the more intensive group, reported Michael K. Gould, MD, of the Kaiser Permanente Bernard J. Tyson School of Medicine in Pasadena, California, and colleagues.

After adjustment, size progression to larger than 20 mm was 7 percentage points (95% CI -2.0 to 15.9) more common in the less intensive group than the more intensive group, which exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of 5 percentage points, but was not statistically significant.

"Although neither group was clearly superior in the main analysis, we cautiously advise guideline developers to consider returning to the prior, more intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules, particularly in younger persons," the authors wrote in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

Indeed, a subgroup analysis showed that tumor progression was significantly more likely among younger patients in the less intensive group.

"We weren't able to validate the less intensive approach reflected in the current guidelines -- we weren't able to demonstrate noninferiority," Gould told MedPage Today.

In addition, "progression in size and stage are more common than one would think, perhaps suggesting that the whole idea of a CT follow-up strategy be reconsidered," he said. "When we see one-third of patients having progression, we need to do better."

Given the frequency of size progression in both groups, "newer approaches to follow-up for patients with small pulmonary nodules, including volumetric measurement, novel biomarkers, and radiomic tools, should be rigorously evaluated," Gould and team wrote.

The "Watch the Spot" trial enrolled 34,686 participants at 14 healthcare systems between March 2017 and July 2019. Mean age was 64.5, and 50.8% were women. All had a newly identified pulmonary nodule measuring 15 mm or less in diameter on a diagnostic or screening chest CT scan, defined as the index scan.

The protocols for less and more intensive CT follow-up were modeled on current and prior recommendations from the Fleischner Society and the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS).

Lung cancer was diagnosed within 27 months of nodule identification in 1.5% of those in the less intensive group and 1.4% of those in the more intensive group.

The median nodule size on the index CT scan was 9 mm, and 70% of all cancers were detected incidentally. More than 25% of lung cancers were diagnosed in participants with nodules measuring 6 mm or less in diameter at the time of detection on the index CT scan.

Median tumor size at diagnosis was 16 mm in the less intensive group compared with 15 mm in the more intensive group, and stage III or IV cancer was somewhat more common in the less intensive group (31.4%) than in the more intensive group (28.6%).

Adherence to protocol-based follow-up was "poor" in both study groups, the authors observed -- 42% in the less intensive group and 45% in the more intensive group. After adjustment among these patients, diagnosis with progression to a tumor size larger than 20 mm was more common in the less intensive group by 14.9 percentage points.

"Adherence is important," Gould observed. "While we're waiting for newer approaches -- whether it's volumetric measurement or novel biomarkers -- the poor adherence we observed in our study represents a very important opportunity for quality improvement."

#5533. WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year

WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Global health insurance costs are set to rise by double digits in 2027 for the second straight year, according to a new survey.

WTW released its latest Global Medical Trends Survey, which estimates that the average gross cost for medical benefits will increase by 10.2% in 2027. This follows a 10.1% increase in 2026 and a 9.8% increase in 2025, according to the report.

In the United States, the cost for medical benefits is expected to rise by 10.3% on average, on par with 2026 and up from a 9.4% increase in 2025. Across regions, the highest increases are expected in the Asia-Pacific, averaging 12.6% in 2027.

The next-highest region was North America, with a projected 10.5% average increase.

The survey was conducted in June and August 2026 and includes responses from 393 insurers offering coverage across 92 countries. Just under half (49%) of those surveyed said they anticipate elevated medical and pharmacy costs to impact them over the next three years, and likely persist beyond that window.

The WTW analysts said this likely means that insurers will remain focused on cost containment and sharing measures in the near future.

"In the US, healthcare costs remain under sustained pressure from new medical technologies, specialty pharmaceuticals, and the rising use of GLP-1 therapies, alongside higher provider costs and the ongoing demands of chronic and complex conditions," said Courtney Stubblefield, strategy and specialty leader in Health & Benefits at WTW in an announcement.

More than three quarters (76%) of the surveyed insurers named new medical technologies as the leading cost drive for both medical and pharmaceutical costs. Sixty-five percent cited provider fee increases, and 45% named pharmaceutical advancements.

Cancer was the leading condition driving costs, the survey found, with 62% naming it as the top cost condition. Sixty-one percent of those surveyed said they have seen an increase in cancer diagnoses among individuals under age 40 when compared to the past two years.

However, when looking at the conditions where costs are growing the most quickly, cardiovascular disease rises to No. 1, cited by 54% of the surveyed insurers. Cancer was second on this ranking, and named by 51%, while diabetes was third at 28%.

"To manage this, employers need a multiyear, multifaceted strategy that addresses pharmacy spending and high-cost conditions—such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes—while keeping care affordable and accessible for employees," Stubblefield said.

#5532. STAT+: AI can analyze X-rays and CT scans to draft radiology reports. Will it make care better, safer?
